summary: In PCEP message exchanges, some objects must be understood and honored. This RFC introduces a way to mark selected objects as optional in stateful PCE operation, so path computation and setup can relax constraints instead of failing when an optional item cannot be satisfied.

eli5.summary: On a to-do list, some things are must-dos and others are nice-to-haves. This lets path-planning computers mark nice-to-haves so one missing item doesn't stop the whole job.

questions: how can stateful pce relax constraints
what is the r flag in pcep

how does stateful pce relax constraints
subtitle: Lets stateful PCEP peers mark objects as optional, so a constraint can be relaxed instead of failing the whole request.

tldr.problem: In stateful PCEP, the P and I flags of objects are set to zero and ignored, so a peer cannot say that a constraint is optional or report that it skipped one.
tldr.mechanism: A new R (RELAX) flag in the STATEFUL-PCE-CAPABILITY TLV lets both peers agree to honor the P and I flags in PCRpt, PCUpd and PCInitiate messages. P set means the object must be processed; P cleared means it is optional; I says an optional object was ignored.
tldr.outcome: Stateful PCE can relax constraints during path computation and setup, and unknown objects are now handled according to the P flag. This updates RFC 8231.

today: RFC 9753 is a Proposed Standard published in April 2025. It updates RFC 8231 and has not been obsoleted or updated by a later RFC.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
In RFC 5440, the P flag (Processing-Rule) in the common object header lets a PCC tell a PCE, in a PCReq message, whether an object must be taken into account during path computation or is optional. The I flag (Ignore) lets the PCE say in a PCRep message whether an optional object was considered.

Stateful PCE (RFC 8231) specifies that the P and I flags are set to zero on transmission and ignored on receipt, since they relate only to path computation requests. This document specifies how these flags can be used in the stateful model, in the PCRpt, PCUpd and PCInitiate (RFC 8281) messages. It updates RFC 8231 on the use of the flags and on handling unknown objects.
sections.eli5: There were already must-do and nice-to-have stickers for some messages. This RFC lets the other messages use the stickers too.

sections.title: Why Optional Objects Help
sections.content:
A PCRpt message carries the intended and actual attribute lists. The intended list could include a METRIC object with the Bound ('B') flag set, as a limiting constraint for the Path Delay Variation metric. If the PCE cannot find a path, it would be useful to say that this constraint can be relaxed, and for the sender to learn that the peer ignored it.

The P and I flags apply to a whole PCEP object. They cannot be applied to individual optional TLVs inside an object.
sections.eli5: Saying 'I would like a path under this delay, but if it is impossible, go ahead without it' needs a way to mark the wish as optional.

sections.title: The R Flag Capability
sections.content:
During PCEP initialization, a PCC sends an Open message whose OPEN object contains the STATEFUL-PCE-CAPABILITY TLV (RFC 8231). This document adds the R (RELAX) flag, bit 17, to that TLV. Set to 1, it says the speaker is willing to handle the P and I flags for objects in stateful messages. Unset, it will not.

Both the PCC and the PCE MUST set the R flag for the relaxation to apply. A speaker that does not set R but receives objects with P or I set MUST ignore the flags.
sections.eli5: Both sides have to say 'I understand the stickers' before anyone starts using them.

sections.title: Handling the P and I Flags
sections.content:
On a session where both peers set R, a set P flag in a PCRpt, PCUpd or PCInitiate message means the receiver MUST take the object into account. A cleared P flag means the object is optional and may be ignored. Mandatory objects must have P set: the LSP and ERO in PCRpt, and the SRP, LSP and ERO in PCUpd and PCInitiate. Otherwise the receiver MUST send a PCErr with Error-Type=10 and Error-value=1. Senders SHOULD set P by default unless local policy marks a constraint as optional or the object only conveys ignorable information.

For delegated LSPs, the PCE can update and mark some objects as ignored even if the PCC set P, or mark them 'must process' even if the PCC did not. The PCC MUST acknowledge with a PCRpt carrying P as the PCE expects.

The I flag reports what happened. A PCE MAY include an ignored optional object in a PCUpd and set I; a PCC MAY do the same in a PCRpt answering a PCUpd or PCInitiate. A cleared I flag means the object was processed. I has no meaning in PCInitiate, where it MUST be set to 0 on transmission and ignored on receipt.
sections.eli5: A must-do sticker means 'you have to do this', a nice-to-have sticker means 'skip it if needed', and a second sticker tells the other side 'I skipped it'.

sections.title: Unknown Object Handling
sections.content: If a speaker does not understand an object with the P flag set, or understands it but decides to ignore it, the entire stateful PCEP message MUST be rejected and a PCErr sent with Error-Type "Unknown Object" or "Not supported object". If P is not set, the speaker can ignore the object and continue processing the message. The LSP Error Code TLV procedure in PCRpt is unchanged.
sections.eli5: If a must-do item is something you cannot do, the whole job is turned down. If it is only a nice-to-have, you carry on.

sections.title: IANA and Manageability
sections.content:
IANA allocated bit 17, named RELAX, in the "STATEFUL-PCE-CAPABILITY TLV Flag Field" registry, referencing RFC 9753.

Implementations SHOULD allow configuring the capability and the LSP constraints that are optional to process, and SHOULD let the operator view the capability. The document adds no new liveness, verification or other-protocol requirements and no extra network impact beyond RFC 5440.
sections.eli5: The official list of sticker numbers got one new entry for this feature.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: On their own, these changes add no new security concerns, and the considerations of RFC 5440, RFC 8231 and RFC 8281 continue to apply. As in RFC 8231, it is RECOMMENDED to activate these extensions only on authenticated and encrypted sessions between PCEs and PCCs of the same administrative authority, using TLS (RFC 8253) following RFC 9325.
sections.eli5: Use a locked, private line between the computers so nobody can tamper with the stickers.

items.label: Must process
items.desc: The receiver MUST take the object into account.

items.label: Optional
items.desc: The receiver can ignore the object.

items.label: Ignored
items.desc: The sender of the message ignored the optional object.
